prompt: Why does Quicksort degrade to Θ(n²) on already-sorted input when the first element is used as pivot?
options: Because comparisons are more expensive on sorted data.
Because the pivot is always the minimum, producing maximally unbalanced partitions and recursion depth n.
Because Quicksort cannot handle sorted input at all and must fall back to Merge Sort.
Because the partition step itself becomes Θ(n²) on sorted input.
explanation: With sorted input and a first-element pivot, every partition splits into one empty side and one side of size n−1. The recursion depth becomes n and the partition costs sum to n + (n−1) + … = Θ(n²). Each individual partition call is still only Θ(n).

prompt: Merge Sort and Quicksort — which two statements are correct?
options: Merge Sort does trivial work while dividing and all the real work while combining; Quicksort is the other way around.
Merge Sort is Θ(n log n) in best, worst and average case.
Merge Sort loses stability when the two sublists being merged have an odd number of elements.
Quicksort needs Θ(n) extra memory, whereas Merge Sort sorts in place.
explanation: The divide/combine asymmetry is the defining contrast ✓, and merging always costs Θ(n) regardless of input order, so Merge Sort has no bad input ✓. Stability depends only on the merge tie-break (favouring the left element), not on sublist parity ✗. The memory claim is inverted: Quicksort is in place, Merge Sort needs the Θ(n) temp array ✗.

prompt: Worst-case behaviour of the sorting algorithms — which two statements are correct?
options: Quicksort has worst case Θ(n²), triggerable by an unlucky pivot choice such as always picking the smallest element.
Merge Sort has worst case Θ(n²) when the list is reverse-sorted.
Choosing the pivot randomly makes Quicksort's Θ(n²) worst case unlikely but does not eliminate it.
Quicksort's worst case disappears entirely once the pivot is chosen randomly.
explanation: Maximally unbalanced splits give Θ(n²) ✓, and randomisation only makes that outcome improbable — an unlucky random sequence can still produce it ✓. Merge Sort is Θ(n log n) on every input ✗, and no pivot rule removes the worst case from the algorithm's *worst-case* analysis ✗.

prompt: The Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison-based sorting — which two statements are correct?
options: Every correct comparison-based sorting algorithm needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
The bound follows from a decision-tree argument: n! orderings require a tree of depth ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).
The bound applies only to unstable sorting algorithms.
A comparison-based algorithm can sort in O(n) worst case by first building a binary search tree.
explanation: The information-theoretic bound holds for every comparison-based sort ✓ and comes from the decision-tree depth ✓. Stability is irrelevant to it ✗. Building a BST does not escape the bound — an unbalanced BST degenerates to height n, giving Θ(n²) total ✗.

prompt: Quicksort's `partition(A, left, right)` with `pivot = A[left]` — which two statements are correct?
options: The returned index q is the split point, and the recursive calls are quicksort(A, left, q) and quicksort(A, q+1, right).
After partitioning, every element in A[left..q] is ≤ pivot and every element in A[q+1..right] is ≥ pivot.
After partitioning, the pivot is guaranteed to sit exactly at index q in its final sorted position.
Partition runs in Θ(n log n) for a subarray of length n.
explanation: This is the Hoare-style partition used in the lecture: it returns q and recurses on [left..q] and [q+1..right] ✓, guaranteeing the two-sided ≤/≥ property ✓. Unlike Lomuto partitioning, Hoare's scheme does *not* place the pivot at its final position ✗. Partition is a single scan, Θ(n) ✗.

prompt: Divide and Conquer — which two statements are correct?
options: The runtime of a D&C algorithm depends only on the complexity of the combine step.
D&C splits a problem into smaller instances of the same problem, solves them recursively and combines the partial solutions.
The recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) captures the cost of a D&C algorithm, with f(n) the divide-plus-combine cost.
A D&C algorithm must split each problem into equally sized subproblems in order to be correct.
explanation: The definition ✓ and the standard recurrence ✓ are correct. The runtime depends on the number and size of subproblems *and* the divide/combine cost — the Master Theorem's whole point is comparing them ✗. Equal-size splitting affects efficiency, never correctness (Quicksort splits unevenly and is still correct) ✗.

prompt: Ranking the three sorts by worst-case complexity — which two statements are correct?
options: Merge Sort Θ(n log n) < Quicksort Θ(n²) = Insertion Sort Θ(n²) is the correct ascending worst-case ranking.
Quicksort and Insertion Sort tie in the worst case, but Quicksort's expected runtime Θ(n log n) beats Insertion Sort's Θ(n²).
Quicksort has a strictly better worst case than Insertion Sort.
Merge Sort and Quicksort tie in the worst case at Θ(n log n).
explanation: Worst cases: Merge Sort Θ(n log n), Quicksort Θ(n²), Insertion Sort Θ(n²) ✓ — so the last two tie, and the tie-break is the *expected* runtime, where Quicksort's Θ(n log n) wins ✓. Options 3 and 4 both contradict Quicksort's Θ(n²) worst case ✗✗.

prompt: Why does Quicksort usually beat Merge Sort in practice despite the same average complexity? Which two statements are correct?
options: Quicksort sorts in place, avoiding the copying into and out of a temp array.
Quicksort has smaller constant factors hidden by the Θ-notation.
Quicksort performs asymptotically fewer comparisons on average.
Quicksort's recursion depth is Θ(log n) in the worst case, unlike Merge Sort's Θ(n).
explanation: In-place operation ✓ and smaller constants ✓ are the practical reasons. Both are Θ(n log n) comparisons on average, so neither is asymptotically fewer ✗. Recursion depth is the reverse: Merge Sort is always Θ(log n), Quicksort can reach Θ(n) in the worst case ✗.
